issues.legal_issue: Acquiring the interests of co-owners in a house through consideration-bearing release deeds constitutes a purchase for purposes of the capital-gains exemption.
material_facts: After selling his own house at a profit giving rise to capital gains, the taxpayer acquired his brothers’ interests in a jointly owned house.
The brothers transferred their interests to the taxpayer by separate release deeds for consideration, which was adjusted against an agreed extra share rather than paid in cash.
The transfers converted the joint ownership of the house into the taxpayer’s separate ownership.
issues.conclusion: The release deeds transferred the brothers’ shares for consideration and therefore amounted to a purchase within the meaning of section 54(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The Court agreed with the High Court and dismissed the Revenue’s petition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54(1) does not require a purchase to be made by cash payment. In the absence of a contextual reason to depart from ordinary usage, purchase includes acquiring property for a price or its monetary equivalent, including consideration paid in kind or adjusted against another obligation. The Court relied on Habshaw Brothers Ltd. v. Mayer, [1956] 3 All ER 833, 835, in support of the meaning of purchase as acquisition for money or money’s worth.

predicates.capital_gains_reinvestment_claim: A person who sells a house seeks capital-gains relief on the basis of acquiring another house.
predicates.ownership_interest_transferred: One or more co-owners transfer their interests in a jointly owned house to the person claiming relief.
predicates.consideration_paid_or_adjusted: The person acquiring the interests gives money or its equivalent as consideration, whether paid directly or satisfied by adjustment.

issues.definition: When a person seeking capital-gains relief after selling a house acquires co-owners’ interests in another jointly owned house for money or its equivalent, the acquisition counts as a purchase.
